[

]

These
Reasons for
Sentence
were delivered as oral reasons. They have since been
edited for distribution.

Introduction

[
2
]

Jan Poepl is before the
court for sentencing following his guilty plea to one count of second degree
murder
contrary
to
s. 235(1)
of the
Criminal
Code,
R.S.C.
1985, c. c-46

[
Code
]. Mr. Poepl entered his
guilty plea on December 15, 2020. The charge relates to the murder of his
former girlfriend, Nicole Hasselmann. The offence occurred on the evening of
November 16, 2018.

[
3
]

Pursuant to
s. 235(1)
of the
Code
, the offence of second degree murder
carries a mandatory
sentence of life imprisonment with no eligibility for parole for at least 10
years. The sole issue before the Court on this sentencing is the determination
of the appropriate period of parole ineligibility.

[
4
]

To
be clear, Mr. Poepl will be subject to a life sentence—that means supervision
for the rest of his life. The decision today on parole ineligibility simply
sets the time frame for when he can apply for parole. Whether he obtains parole
is a decision for the Parole Board of Canada to make when they assess
suitability for release:
R. v. Danjou
,
2020 BCSC 1820
at para.
10
;
R.
v. Meers
,
2018 BCSC 465
at para.
12
.

[
5
]

The
Crown seeks a period of 15 years’ parole ineligibility. The defence contends
that given the circumstances of the offence and of this offender, that the
period of parole ineligibility ought to be set at the minimum 10-year period.

[
6
]

The
nature of the offence and the circumstances surrounding its commission are, to
be blunt, horrific and brutal. Another descriptor sometimes used in the
jurisprudence that is apt in the overall circumstances of this case is “stark
horror”.

[
7
]

In a grief-stricken victim
impact statement delivered by Ms. Hasselmann’s aunt, Deanna Smith asks “WHY!
WHY! WHY! did Jan take Nicole away from us all”? To the horror of everyone who
watched Mr. Poepl’s selfie video (Ex. #3) taken moments after he inflicted 47
stab wounds to Ms. Hasselmann, and as she lay in the passenger seat of the
rental vehicle Mr. Poepl was driving, gasping for air, we learned the
disturbing answer to this profoundly troubling question. Ms. Hasselmann had to
die because, according to Mr. Poepl, she disrespected him. It seems that the
disrespect was because she continued to communicate with and date other men,
and because she did not want a romantic relationship with Mr. Poepl unless he
dealt with his anger management issues.

[
8
]

Ms. Hasselmann ended
her relationship with Mr. Poepl on November 7, 2018—9 days before her death—but
continued to communicate with Mr. Poepl and, on the evening of her death, spend
time with him. She made it clear to Mr. Poepl that she was not interested in a
relationship with him unless and until he could control his temper. This point
is made patently clear in the text messages she exchanged with Mr. Poepl
between September 2, 2018, and November 7, 2018, as included in the agreed statement
of facts filed at the sentence hearing.

[
9
]

Ms. Hasselmann was a
bright, vivacious, independent and beloved young woman. She wanted to live her
life on her terms, as she was entitled to do. She wanted a relationship where
she felt safe and not subjected to a man with an explosive temper. In ending
the relationship on November 7, 2018, Ms. Hasselmann told Mr. Poepl she did not
trust him, she had seen him at his worst, and wrote “you are physically,
sexually, emotionally abusive, you call me names, u blew it with my son, u blew
it with his dad, and you threatened me too many times”.

[
10
]

Sadly, Mr. Poepl’s
jealousy, rage and single-minded pursuit of Ms. Hasselmann, blaming their
relationship difficulties on her and her seeing another man, is an all too
familiar and profoundly disturbing theme both in the courts and in the broader
realm of society. Mr. Poepl intentionally stabbed Ms. Hasselmann because he
felt she was disrespecting him. His reasoning appears to be the sadly familiar
and disturbing trope “If I can’t have her, nobody can.” Violence against women
cannot be tolerated in any form. Intimate partner violence cannot be tolerated
in any form. It is abhorrent conduct that must be denounced in the strongest of
terms.

[
11
]

Mr. Poepl’s decision to
take the life of his former girlfriend must be met with a denunciatory sentence
that represents “a symbolic, collective statement that the offender’s conduct
should be punished for encroaching on our society’s basic code of values as
enshrined within our substantive law”:
R. v. C.A.M.
,
1996 CanLII 230 (SCC)
,
[1996] 1 S.C.R.
500
;
R. v. Atwal
,
2006 BCCA 493
at para.
21
.

The Legal Framework

[
12
]

Pursuant to
ss. 745
(c) and
745.4
of the
Code
,
where an offender is convicted of second degree murder, the court may set the
period of parole ineligibility between 10 and 25 years. The legal framework is
not in dispute in this case; where Mr. Poepl falls on the wide spectrum of
parole ineligibility is what is at issue.

[
13
]

In the leading case of
R. v. Shropshire
,

1995 CanLII 47 (SCC)
,
[1995] 4 S.C.R. 227
, Justice Iacobucci, writing for the Court, held at para.18:

The determination under s. 744 [now s.
745.4] is thus a very fact-sensitive process. The factors to be considered in
fixing an extended period of parole ineligibility are:

(1) the character
of the offender;

(2) the nature of
the offence; and

(3) the circumstances
surrounding the commission of the offence;

all bearing in
mind the discretionary power conferred on the trial judge.

[
14
]

Parole ineligibility is
part of the punishment and an important element of the sentencing in the
context of an offence for second degree murder:
R. v. Bhandher
,
2010
BCSC 1812
at para.
3
;
R. v. Reierson
,
2007 BCSC 541
at para.
4
.

[
15
]

As noted above,
s.
745.4
of the
Code
sets out the factors for consideration in determining
whether to increase parole eligibility beyond 10 years. As Mr. Poepl’s case
involved a guilty plea, there was no trial and therefore no s. 745.2 jury
recommendation to consider.

[
16
]

The purpose and
principles of sentencing outlined in
ss. 718
,
718.1
, and
718.2
of the
Code

remain relevant in setting the period of parole ineligibility under
s. 745.4
.
Thus, the factors to be taken into account when increasing parole ineligibility
include denunciation, deterrence, and future dangerousness. Proportionality is
always a consideration as well:
Reierson
at para.
4
. As is the parity
principle. Finally, the principle of retribution also informs the sentencing objectives
in a case such as this one. Retribution, which is neither vengeance nor
denunciation, requires a sentence to “properly reflect the moral
blameworthiness of the particular offender”:
R. v. Dolman
,
2017 BCSC
2564
at para.
11
.

[
17
]

Sentencing is a
fact-sensitive process and each case is unique. However, as Justice Donald
explained
in
R. v. Cerra
,
2004 BCCA 594
, the appropriate range of
sentence should be assessed considering other similar sentencing decisions (the
parity principle):

[17]      It
has often been said that sentencing is an individualized process and
comparisons with other cases are difficult. But difficult as they may be,
comparisons must be made when reviewing sentences for fitness. Patterns may
emerge from an examination of sentencing decisions. I have discerned a pattern
from decisions of this Court suggesting, in broad terms, the following: parole
eligibility greater than 10 years is justified when there is some particularly
aggravating feature; for a penalty of greater than 15 years, egregious
circumstances of a higher order of moral culpability are present. So in this
case, the savage and prolonged beating raises the penalty above 10 years
eligibility. That much is conceded by Mr. Cerra's counsel who urged us to go no
higher than 15 years in adjusting the penalty. The key issue is whether there
was something more in this case lifting it into a still higher level of blameworthiness.

[
18
]

After reviewing a number of authorities, Donald J.A. determined in
Cerra

at para.
26
that there appeared to be two main “ranges” for parole
ineligibility in second degree murder cases where parole is extended beyond the
statutory minimum of 10 years.

[
19
]

The first elevated range is from 12 to 15 years and represents cases
with some particularly aggravating feature.

[
20
]

The second and more elevated range is from 15 to 20 years. This latter
range relates to cases with extremely aggravating facts or egregious
circumstances placing the offender at the highest order of moral culpability or
dangerousness. Parole ineligibility periods beyond 20 years are usually reserved
for exceptional cases. It is not engaged in this case.

[
21
]

Of course, the wide discretion granted to sentencing judges is
informed by the case law and general ranges of sentences for particular
offences. However, while courts must consider ranges, the jurisprudence from
the Supreme Court of Canada is clear that “ranges” are guidelines, not hard and
fast rules or “straightjackets.” So long as the sentence imposed is in
accordance with the principles and objectives of sentencing and is
proportionate to the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of
the offender, a sentence outside the regular range is not necessarily unfit:
R.
v. Nasogaluak
,
2010 SCC 6
at para.
44
;
R. v. Lacasse,

2015 SCC
64
at paras.
56–72
;
R. v. Friesen
,
2020 SCC 9
at paras.
37–38
, 108.

[
22
]

It is important to reiterate that the judicial function in a case
such as Mr. Poepl’s is one of sentencing and not of parole determination—upon
expiry of the parole ineligibility period, it still remains for the parole
authorities to determine the offender's suitability for release:
Danjou

at
para.
10
;
Bhandher
at para.
8
;
Reierson
at para.
5
.

[
23
]

In
R. v. Bennight
,
2012 BCCA 461
, our Court of Appeal
confirmed its earlier decision in
Cerra
that recognized the two broad
groupings of cases where parole ineligibility is extended beyond 10 years
(periods from 12 to 15 years and periods of 15 to 20 years, with the latter
group relating to cases at the highest order of moral culpability or
dangerousness).

[
24
]

Bennight
is also
useful in identifying the general principles that apply when considering
whether to impose a period of parole ineligibility above the 10-year minimum.
Justice MacKenzie, writing for the Court of Appeal, enumerated the applicable
principles at para. 18:

The
following principles apply to the decision to impose an extended period of
parole ineligibility:

•

Under
s. 745.4 of the
Criminal Code
, the sentencing judge must consider the
character of the offender, the nature of the offence, the circumstances
surrounding the commission of the offence, and the recommendation of the jury
(if any).

•

The
general sentencing principles of denunciation and deterrence and the judge’s
assessment of the offender’s future dangerousness are relevant factors:
R.
v. Shropshire
,
1995 CanLII 47 (SCC)
,
[1995] 4 S.C.R. 227
,
102 C.C.C. (3d) 193
.

•

Parole
ineligibility greater than 10 years is justified when there is some
particularly aggravating feature:
Cerra
, at para.
17
(per Donald J.A.).

•

There
are two broad groupings of cases where parole ineligibility is extended beyond
10 years: parole ineligibility periods from 12 to 15 years and parole
ineligibility periods from 15 to 20 years. The latter group of cases relates to
cases at the highest order of moral culpability or dangerousness:
Cerra
,
at para.
26
(per Donald J.A.).

•

The
possibility of a parole ineligibility period greater than 20 years remains in
exceptional circumstances:
Cerra
, at para.
36
(per Ryan J.A.).

•

Orders
extending the period of parole ineligibility are highly discretionary and are
part of the sentence pursuant to
s. 673
of the
Criminal Code
. Such
orders are therefore appealed pursuant to s. 687(1). An appellant court
should only interfere with a trial judge’s sentencing order if the court is
convinced it is not fit or it is clearly unreasonable:
Shropshire
, at
paras.
47-48
.

•

The
wide discretion granted to sentencing judges is fettered by the case law and
general ranges of sentences for particular offences. However, while courts must
consider ranges, they are guidelines rather than strict rules. A sentence
outside the regular range is not necessarily unfit, if it is in accordance with
the principles and objectives of sentencing:
R. v. Nasogaluak
,
2010 SCC
6
,
[2010] 1 S.C.R. 206
at para.
44
.

•

Similarly,
the two groups of parole ineligibility cases
described in
Cerra
are
intended as guidelines, not as binding categories within which a particular
case must be placed:
R. v. White
,
2011 BCCA 328
at para.
24
.

[
25
]

I will consider those principles as I proceed with my analysis.

[
26
]

Before discussing the character of the offender, I will turn first
to consider the other two statutory factors enumerated in s. 745.4 of the
Code—
the
nature of the offence and the circumstances of its commission.

Nature of the Offence and
Circumstances of Its Commission

[
27
]

The nature of the offence and the circumstances of its commission
are outlined in graphic detail in Ex. #2, the agreed statement of facts, filed
at the sentencing hearing and read into the record. My summary of the offence
and the circumstances of its commission are derived largely from that document.

[
28
]

Not included in the agreed statement of facts but fundamentally
apparent from it and from the submissions made at the sentence hearing is the fact
that, in so far as the nature of the offence is concerned, in my view, it is
akin to spousal homicide cases—it is an example of domestic violence that resulted
in the death of the offender’s former intimate partner. It occurred in the
context of the dissolution of their relationship. The motive appears to be
jealousy and rage over the deceased’s decision to exercise personal autonomy,
end their romantic relationship and date other men.

[
29
]

The circumstances surrounding the actual commission of the offence
are horrific.

[
30
]

Ms. Hasselmann was 34 years old when she was killed by Mr. Poepl.
She worked as Special Education Assistant at Templeton High School.

[
31
]

Ms. Hasselmann was a single mother to a 10-year-old boy. Her son
lived with her full-time. Although Ms. Hasselmann was divorced from her husband,
it is apparent that they still had an amicable relationship and worked to
co-parent their young son. Both parents were involved in their son’s
extra-curricular passion: hockey. Their son was a talented goalie, indeed
according to Dina Bezic’s victim impact statement, Ms. Hasselmann’s son was the
top goalie for the division he played in Burnaby Minor. Ms. Bezic is the mother
of a teammate on the hockey team and was a friend of Ms. Hasselmann.

[
32
]

At the time of the offence, Mr. Poepl was employed as a real estate
agent and was also involved with his brother in a renovation project of a
residence on College Parkway in Port Moody. Mr. Poepl lived in that residence.

[
33
]

The contextual background to the offence is this. At the time of her
death, Ms. Hasselmann and Mr. Poepl had been in an “on again, off again”
dating relationship of approximately seven years’ duration. In the two years
that preceded her death, Ms. Hasselmann had been involved in another romantic
relationship, which made Mr. Poepl extremely jealous. Mr. Poepl’s actions
included following Ms. Hasselmann, posting compromising photographs of her
on WhatsApp, and checking her cell phone when they were together. He was
physically abusive with her on at least one occasion when she was checking her
cell phone. He repeatedly told Ms. Hasselmann that she was “disrespecting him”
by carrying on with the other man.

[
34
]

During their relationship, Ms. Hasselmann repeatedly urged Mr. Poepl
to seek counselling as she did not like the way he treated her. In particular,
she did not like how he would “fly into a jealous rage” over her relationship
with another man. Ms.  Hasselmann repeatedly told Mr. Poepl that he scared
her when he behaved this way and that his lack of self control and temper were
the issues driving them apart.

[
35
]

Included in the agreed statement of facts is a series of text
messages between Mr. Poepl and Ms. Hasselmann spanning the period of September
2, 2018 to November 7, 2018. The text messages demonstrate Ms. Hasselmann’s
efforts to try and make Mr. Poepl see that his anger, jealousy and abusive
behaviour was what was driving them apart, not her relationship with another
man.

[
36
]

On November 7, 2018, Ms. Hasselmann ended her relationship with both
Mr. Poepl and the other man, although she continued to communicate with
both men. Mr. Poepl wanted to reconcile but Ms. Hasselmann was steadfast that
she was not interested in a relationship with him unless and until he could
control his temper.

[
37
]

After the break up with Mr. Poepl and the other man, Ms. Hasselmann
started online dating.

[
38
]

On the evening of the offence, November 16, 2018, Ms. Hasselmann’s
son was scheduled to play hockey at 7 p.m. in Burnaby. His father took him to
the rink. Ms. Hasselmann planned to attend the game but first arranged to meet
Mr. Poepl at his home at 6:00 p.m. Mr. Poepl was going to drop Ms. Hasselmann
at the rink at 7:00 p.m. so she could watch her son play hockey.

[
39
]

Mr. Poepl picked Ms. Hasselmann up at 6:05 p.m. and then drove to
his home. Sometime between 6:18 p.m. and 6:39 p.m. Ms. Hasselmann learned that
her son was not going to be playing hockey that evening. Consequently, she did
not go to the rink but continued her visit with Mr. Poepl.

[
40
]

At 6:20 p.m. Ms. Hasselmann received a text message from a man she
had met online. At 6:52 p.m. she received a text message from the other man she
had been dating but whom she had also broken up with on November 7, 2018. The
last text message Ms. Hasselmann sent was at 6:45 p.m., to her ex-husband. At
some point in this time period, Mr. Poepl and Ms. Hasselmann returned to the
rental vehicle that Mr. Poepl was driving.

[
41
]

By 7:31 p.m., Mr. Poepl had stabbed Ms. Hasselmann 47 times as she
sat in the passenger seat of his vehicle. He used two knives that he happened
to have in his vehicle. The knives, purchased in September 2018, were tactical
folding knives designed for military use. Mr. Poepl had the knives in his
vehicle for his own protection and carried them with him for those occasions when
he went into the Downtown Eastside to buy drugs.

[
42
]

Ms. Hasselmann sustained 47 incision / stab wounds. Almost all of
them were to the left side of her body—20 of the wounds were to the front and
back of her left shoulder with the deepest wound being approximately 13–14 cm
in depth. Ms. Hasselmann had defensive wounds in a number of places
including on her left upper forearm, her right forearm, her upper back and her
hands. None of the stab wounds severed vital organs; however, the most serious
stab wound was to her thyroid. This stab wound, 2 cm wide and 6–7 cm deep, was
to the front of her neck and penetrated the left lobe of her thyroid. It was
potentially fatal as the perforation of the thyroid lobe caused the release of
thyroid hormones, which made it difficult for Ms. Hasselmann to breathe.

[
43
]

After Mr. Poepl finished stabbing Ms. Hasselmann, he removed his
blood stained jacket and then turned on his cell phone camera and filmed Ms.
Hasselmann as she gasped for air. She can be heard to say that she needs air
and Mr. Poepl states words to the effect of “that’s the worst, I know.” In a
measured and calm voice, Mr. Poepl states he has done the worst thing. Ms.
Hasselmann tries to comfort him, tells him it is ok and that she loved him.
Remarkably, Mr. Poepl continues in his calm, matter-of-fact manner and tells
Ms. Hasselmann words to the effect of “yes, I know, but you never treated me
with respect.” He then tells Ms. Hasselmann, “you just took, took, took
from me—you disrespected me.” What is astonishing about the video is the
absolute absence of remorse, regret or panic in Mr. Poepl’s presentation. It is
shocking in its total absence of empathy or concern for what he has just done
to the woman he purported to love.

[
44
]

After repeatedly stabbing Ms. Hasselmann and then filming her in her
endangered condition, Mr. Poepl engaged in a series of actions that can only be
described as callous, cruel and self-absorbed. First, he did not phone anyone
or endeavour to obtain medical assistance for Ms. Hasselmann who was in obvious
distress and grave danger. It is not clear from the agreed statement of facts
where the rental vehicle was located when this stabbing occurred, although
there is reference to the fact that there were two fire halls and a hospital
nearby, which Mr. Poepl failed to take Ms. Hasselmann to for medical
assistance.

[
45
]

Mr. Poepl then engaged in a series of communications with his
brother, either by talking with him on his cell phone or texting him. Between
7:33 p.m. and 7:45 p.m., Mr. Poepl had spoken to his brother on the phone twice
and had sent him six text messages. He never advised his brother of what he had
just done to Ms. Hasselmann, although he appeared to be concerned about
his brother’s family circumstances and whether he was inconveniencing him at
the time of the conversations.

[
46
]

Sometime around 8:00 p.m. Mr. Poepl returned to his residence,
leaving Ms. Hasselmann in the front seat of his vehicle. Although Ms.
Hasselmann’s cell phone cover was found inside Mr. Poepl’s vehicle, her cell
phone has never been recovered. Also around this time, neighbours heard
prolonged honking from a vehicle near Mr. Poepl’s home.

[
47
]

Between 8:00 p.m. and 9:21 p.m. Mr. Poepl engaged in a series of
online banking and shopping transactions. He also emailed his resignation to
the managing broker where he practiced as a real estate agent.

[
48
]

Sometime after 9:21 p.m. Mr. Poepl returned to his rental vehicle
and started to drive. At 9:38 p.m., he spoke with his brother and told him what
he had done to Ms. Hasselmann and confirmed she was still alive. Mr. Poepl’s
brother repeatedly implored him to get medical assistance for Ms. Hasselmann,
whose voice he could hear in the background. Mr. Poepl advised his brother that
it was too late, Ms. Hasselmann was dying and he was not going to jail. Mr.
Poepl’s brother offered to join him and assist him but Mr. Poepl, who by this
time was driving along the Barnett Highway, refused, lied about his whereabouts,
and threatened to kill himself. The call with his brother ended at 9:44 p.m.

[
49
]

As Mr. Poepl ended his phone call with his brother, he accelerated
his vehicle to 167 km/h and then intentionally struck a light standard,
shearing it. He continued driving and aimed his vehicle at a second light
standard which he struck and sheared. Mr. Poepl never used the vehicle’s brakes
in this phase of his driving. The vehicle became airborne and ended up in a
ditch south of the Barnett Highway in Burnaby, BC.

[
50
]

Ms. Hasselmann was not wearing a seat belt at the time of Mr.
Poepl’s intentional motor vehicle accident. She struck her head against the
front windshield and was then ejected from the vehicle through the back
windscreen before the vehicle landed in its final resting position.

[
51
]

Mr. Poepl exited the driver’s seat and moved to the front passenger
seat where he was found by first responders. Initially, the first responders
were unaware that there was another person associated to the vehicle. Ms.
Hasselmann’s body was discovered approximately 10 minutes later, about 45–100
feet away from the rear of the vehicle.

[
52
]

In addition to the life-threatening injuries sustained as a result
of the stabbing, Ms. Hasselmann was grievously injured as a result of Mr.
Poepl’s intentional car accident. Ten of the 12 ribs on the left side of her
body were broken, likely when she was ejected from the vehicle. The broken ribs
punctured both her heart and a lung which caused immediate massive bleeding.
Ms. Hasselmann died from the combination of (i) sharp force trauma to her
thyroid caused by Mr. Poepl’s initial stabbing and (ii) the lacerations to her
heart when her broken ribs punctured her heart caused by Mr. Poepl’s
intentional motor vehicle collision with the light standards on Barnett Hwy.

[
53
]

It is admitted that Mr. Poepl intentionally killed Ms. Hasselmann by
stabbing her multiple times and then purposefully driving his vehicle at a high
rate of speed into two light standards. In effect, Mr. Poepl killed Ms.
Hasselmann twice.

[
54
]

Mr. Poepl was hospitalized after his accident, having sustained a
fractured left shoulder. Upon his discharge from hospital, he was immediately
arrested. On November 29, 2018, Mr. Poepl provided a statement to the police.
In it he expressed surprise that he was being investigated for murder stating
that Ms. Hasselmann had died in “a tragic car accident”.

[
55
]

Mr. Poepl’s comments to his brother, coupled with the nature of his driving
and intentional collision with two light standards as well as his statement to
the police upon his arrest supports the inference, and I find, that Mr. Poepl
was intent not only upon trying to kill himself because he did not want to go
to jail, but also to make Ms. Hasselmann’s death look like a tragic car
accident.

Background and Character of the
Offender

[
56
]

Mr. Poepl is now 34 years of age. He was 31 years old when he killed
Ms. Hasselmann.

[
57
]

Mr. Poepl has no criminal record. He has been gainfully employed for
most of his adult life.

[
58
]

Mr. Poepl was born and raised in Germany. He has a younger sister, a
twin brother and another brother. Mr. Poepl’s parents and sister still live in
Germany but travel frequently to Canada to visit Mr. Poepl and his brothers.
Indeed, in 2012 his little sister, 12 years his junior, came to Canada to live
with him and do a year of high school in the Lower Mainland.

[
59
]

Growing up, Mr. Poepl appeared to have an unremarkable childhood,
both parents were employed and the children well provided for. However, Mr.
Poepl and his parents experienced friction in his teenage years, no doubt in
part caused by his resort to using drugs that became a full-blown addiction. By
the time he was 15 years old he was using ecstasy, cocaine and speed (amphetamines).

[
60
]

Despite his drug addiction, Mr. Poepl graduated from high school in
Germany, did an apprenticeship in the IT sector and worked in that capacity
until he was 22 years old.

[
61
]

In 2008 when he was 22 years of age, Mr. Poepl decided to move to
Canada, in part in an effort to turn his life around and “clean up” from his
addiction issues. He was largely successful in weaning himself from hard drugs
and confined his drug use to “dope”, which I take to mean marihuana and its
derivatives.

[
62
]

Upon his arrival in Canada, Mr. Poepl found employment in the
construction industry both in the Lower Mainland of British Columbia and in
Alberta. Mr. Poepl excelled at this and quickly became a supervisor and foreman
on large infrastructure projects including highway building and the
construction of the Olympic Park in Whistler, BC

[
63
]

In 2014, Mr. Poepl was involved in a serious car accident. He was a
passenger in a motor vehicle that collided with a tractor trailer. He had a
lengthy rehabilitation. The injuries he sustained in that accident no doubt
played a role in his decision to work in a different, less physically demanding
industry. In 2014 he obtained his realtor’s licence and was employed with
Re/Max Central as a real estate agent. By 2017 he had been named a member of
the Medallion Club, a designation indicating that he was in the top 10% of
realtors in the Lower Mainland.

[
64
]

Mr. Poepl managed to stay away from hard drugs for a number of
years, but in 2017, as his relationship with Ms. Hasselmann began to founder,
he returned to using cocaine and other hard drugs. Mr. Poepl was unable to cope
with the withdrawal of Ms. Hasselmann’s attention and the dissolution of their
relationship. He became obsessed with her as the text messages in Ex. #2
clearly demonstrate. His consumption of hard drugs only exacerbated his mental
and emotional decomposition during the last two years of his relationship with
Ms. Hasselmann.

[
65
]

Mr. Poepl tried to cope with his addiction issues and get them under
control. At Ms. Hasselmann’s urging, he went to Clearmind International to try
and work on his addiction issues. It helped for a short period of time but ultimately
was unsuccessful. In the days and weeks leading up to the offence, Mr. Poepl’s
addiction issues and his unresolved mental health issues took over his life. Mr.
Poepl believes he consumed cocaine at some point during the evening of the
offence, but no clear indication was given as to when, vis-à-vis his meeting
with Ms. Hasselmann.

[
66
]

Counsel for Mr. Poepl was clear that he was not suggesting that this
was a mitigating factor; it is not in these circumstances. However, it is a
contextual factor to explain what was going on in Mr. Poepl’s life at the time
he killed Ms. Hasselmann.

[
67
]

Mr. Poepl has had considerable time to reflect upon and try to
understand his behaviour in the time leading up to the end of their
relationship and in committing this offence. He recognizes now that he engaged
in very poor behaviour and failed to take prosocial steps to try and improve
himself at the time. He takes full responsibility for what he has done.

[
68
]

Mr. Poepl has demonstrated remorse not only to his family and
friends but also in his genuine apology to Ms. Hasselmann’s family and friends that
he made in court. Understandably, this may never be enough for Ms. Hasselmann’s
community of family and friends.

[
69
]

I accept that Mr. Poepl is genuinely remorseful for what he has done
and that he will live with it for the rest of his life. What persuades me
further in accepting that Mr. Poepl is genuinely remorseful are the two letters
of support from men of faith that Mr. Poepl has been working with since his
detention in custody for this offence.

[
70
]

The first letter is from Rick MacAhonic, the chaplain at the Surrey
Pretrial Services Centre (SPSC). He runs the Spiritual Development Program at
SPSC. Chaplain MacAhonic first met Mr. Poepl in July 2019 and was veritably
impressed with the truthfulness and honesty of Mr. Poepl’s religious assertions
and his willingness to examine his life; something Chaplain MacAhonic described
as unusual and rare, given the environment within which he works. Mr. Poepl is
the only person that the chaplain has encountered who has worked through all 30
booklets that comprise “The Basics of Judaism” book. Chaplain MacAhonic closed
his letter with this observation:

During my time working as a chaplain, I
have counselled many individuals from all walks of life. Because of this
history, I’ve developed a keen sense of assessing a person’s character and can
readily detect when I’m being “played.” In the case of your client, I’ve never
experienced this. I’ve always found him to [be] truthful and honest and what I
would consider a “genuine article.” I believe the steps he has taken to
minimize the trauma to those affected by his actions, is a testament to his
repentant attitude. His commitment to better himself is evident in all that he
has undertaken while spending his time here at SPSC. I believe this attitude
will continue with him in the future and will serve him well, and given the
right opportunities, will provide him with endless possibilities for improving
himself and the community he finds himself in.

[
71
]

The second letter is
from Rabbi Jonathan Schtroks, the Director of the Centre for Judaism in Surrey,
BC. Rabbi Schtroks volunteers his time at SPSC and has been involved in prison
visitations since 1980, first in the United States and more recently in Canada.
Mr. Poepl and Rabbi Schtroks have been meeting on a weekly basis, for more than
a year. Indeed, their meetings used to be in person prior to COVID-19. Rabbi Schtroks
outlines that he has been struck by the introspection that Mr. Poepl has
demonstrated and the responsibility that he accepts for his grave actions. He
closes his letter with this poignant observation:

As I began, Jan’s attitude from the first
time I met him, until the present, was quite a contrast to the attitudes of
denial, system-blaming and regret – that one was caught – that one usually
experiences. I have also met with Jan’s family, who are very aware and
supportive of Jan’s path of personal and spiritual growth. Jan will not be
alone in his spiritual journey. It is my hope, with the utmost sensitivity to
the raw wound that will never disappear, that all of those suffering will take
a fraction of solace in that Jan’s humanity has been shaken to the core, and
Jan wishes he could soften their living hell – even a little.

[
72
]

In addition to these
two letters of support from the chaplain and the rabbi, Mr. Poepl’s family
support him. His brothers were present for the sentencing hearing as was his
mother who travelled from Germany to support her son. Mr. Poepl’s parents,
his sister and brother-in-law and a friend have all filed letters of support.
They universally express their shock, horror and deep sadness at the offence
committed by Mr. Poepl. They condemn his actions in the strongest of terms but
they also stand by Mr. Poepl describing him as cheerful, friendly, having a big
heart and a caring and generous personality. For them, Mr. Poepl’s actions are
completely out of character from the man they know and love.

[
73
]

To Mr. Poepl’s credit,
he has been open and honest with his friends and family about his actions in
this offence, repeatedly expressing remorse, deep regret and pain for his
actions and is fully aware of the impact of what he has done.

[
74
]

As a result of this
offence, Mr. Poepl has returned to his Jewish faith and undertaken a fairly
lengthy and deep examination of himself and his faith and his need to atone for
what he has done in murdering Ms. Hasselmann. The two letters of support from
the chaplain and the rabbi that I have already referred to are powerful
confirmatory evidence of this development.

[
75
]

More proof of Mr.
Poepl’s deep commitment to make positive changes include the letter from Jeff
Sharun, the Concurrent Disorders Counsellor at SPSC, with whom Mr. Poepl has
been working in both one-on-one counselling sessions and in group counselling
sessions for the “Right Living Unit” located at SPSC—a positive living unit that
houses only 10 inmates who have committed themselves to personal growth and
development. Mr. Poepl has been doing the one-on-one work with Mr. Sharun
since June 2020 and the group work since August 2020.

[
76
]

The Life Skills
Facilitator at SPSC—a man identified as Gagan—also provided a letter of support
outlining the positive work that Mr. Poepl has engaged in since May 2020. The
facilitator describes Mr. Poepl as attending the sessions and being motivated, and
showing curiosity, understanding and passion. He also describes Mr. Poepl as
highly encouraging of others on the unit to participate to the best of their
ability.

[
77
]

In addition to the
observations of Mr. Poepl by the staff working at SPSC, it is apparent that Mr.
Poepl has worked hard, as evidenced by the various certificates of achievement
filed at the sentence hearing. Mr. Poepl has completed the following programs:

•

Living Without Violence – completed two times,
once in 2019 and once in 2020;

•

Substance Abuse Management – completed two
times, once in 2019 and once in 2020;

•

Life Skills Program – completed in August 2020;
and,

•

Essential Skills to Success – all 18 modules
completed by July 11, 2020;

[
78
]

Thus, as one would
anticipate and in keeping with Mr. Poepl’s overall personality, the materials
from SPSC establish that Mr. Poepl is a hardworking, polite, pleasant and
respectful inmate who gets along well with peers and staff.

[
79
]

The most concerning
aspect of Mr. Poepl’s character is his inability to have formed a healthy,
respectful relationship with Ms. Hasselmann. His anger, jealousy and
possessiveness as evidenced in the agreed statement of facts demonstrates that
at the time of the offence he had an inability to accept boundaries and
rejection. Mr. Poepl’s obsession with Ms. Hasselmann and his inability to
accept she did not want a romantic relationship with him unless and until he
dealt with his anger issues is a troubling feature of his personality and
character.

[
80
]

Finally, the ferocity
of his attack upon Ms. Hasselmann as she sat with him in his vehicle is another
troubling feature that is indicative of significant anger management issues.
This will need to be addressed and worked upon by Mr. Poepl over the coming
years of his imprisonment. The only conclusion I can reach about Mr. Poepl’s
character in so far as his failure to render or obtain assistance for Ms. Hasselmann
after he stabbed her so many times is that this is very concerning. Suffice to
say the lack of empathy or compassion or concern about what he had done and his
callous indifference to Ms. Hasselmann’s condition as he left her in the
vehicle to slowly bleed to death for a couple of hours before finishing
everything off with an intentional motor vehicle accident is very disturbing.

Victim Impact Statements

[
81
]

Pursuant to
s. 722
of
the
Code
, I have taken into account the 35 victim impact statements that
were filed in this matter. Collectively, the statements describe the
devastating harm done to and the catastrophic loss sustained by Ms. Hasselmann’s
family, friends, work colleagues, students and community as a result of her
death. They too are victims as defined in
s. 2
of the
Code
.

[
82
]

“She was my everything”
would be a heart breaking, devastating comment to read in any victim impact
statement submitted in a sentencing where a criminal offence has resulted in
the death of loved one. It is exponentially more profound and haunting to read
it in the print of an 11-year-old boy whose childhood died the day Mr. Poepl
murdered the young boy’s mother.

[
83
]

It is extremely difficult to adequately
capture in words the enormity of the tragedy and the far-reaching consequences
wrought by Ms. Hasselmann’s senseless and needless death.
In
R. v. Hunter
,

2016 BCSC 796
, Justice Holmes (as she then was) had this observation about the
effects of the offence of murder:

[43]

Murder has powerful and far-reaching effects. Family and friends of
the deceased carry the heaviest loads of grief, loss, and regret. But others
with no direct association to the deceased find their lives changed also. Members
of the community wonder whether they too, or those they care about, may be at
risk. The quality of life in the community inevitably declines.

Those observations
are equally apposite here.

[
84
]

As I just noted, 35
victim impact statements were filed on this sentencing hearing—16 from
immediate and extended family members, and 19 from friends, co-workers, a
parent of a student that Ms. Hasselmann assisted at Templeton High School, and
friends of the family.

[
85
]

Joe and Carmine
Porciello, Ms. Hasselmann’s father and brother, as well as Deanna Smith, Ms. Hasselmann’s
aunt, and Ashley Engelson, a very close friend of Ms. Hasselmann, all read out
their victim impact statement in court. Their accounts were each intensely
moving and emotional. All 35 victim impact statements are eloquent letters that
speak both to the joy that Ms. Hasselmann brought to the lives of her family,
friends and co-workers, and the unfathomable grief and emptiness of the shattered
lives they now experience in light of her death.

[
86
]

The victim impact
statements establish how profoundly many lives have been shattered by the
senseless death of Ms. Hasselmann. Much like the situation
in
R. v. Nguyen
,

2014 BCSC 338
, the impact of the offence on the Porciello and Hasselmann
families is sudden, tragic, far-reaching and unending. The family was a
tightly-knit one. At one moment living in relatively close proximity to each
other, and the next, as a result of this needless stabbing and intentional motor
vehicle accident, a mother and father have lost a beloved daughter, a young son
has lost an adored mother, a brother has lost a cherished sibling, and the
community of friends and family of Ms. Hasselmann have been forever tragically
affected. By all accounts, Ms. Hasselmann was the sun and centre of the
universe for everyone who filed a victim impact statement, and no doubt many
others. The extinguishment of this shining sun in their galaxy, through her
death, has sucked everyone she knew into a black hole of seemingly unending grief—a
giant chasm of emptiness and sadness.

Positions of Counsel

Crown Counsel

[
87
]

In the case
at bar, the Crown asserts that when the nature of the offence and the circumstances
surrounding the commission of this murder and the character and background of
Mr. Poepl are considered, the period of parole ineligibility should be set at 15
years. The Crown contends that the circumstances of this case are as close to
first degree murder as one can get without that offence being charged.
Accordingly, Mr. Poepl actually fits within the elevated 15–20 year parole
ineligibility range. What places him at the bottom of that range, contends the
Crown, is his guilty plea, his acceptance of responsibility in this case, and
his sparing the family and friends of Ms. Hasselmann from having to go through
the gruelling ordeal of a trial.

[
88
]

Counsel for
the Crown relied on the following cases to support their position:

•

R. v.
Cerra
,
2004
BCCA 594
– 20 years’ parole ineligibility upheld;

•

R. v.
Trotman
,

2007 BCCA 209
– 20 years’ parole ineligibility upheld;

•

R. v.
Purdy,

2012
BCCA 272
– 19 years’ parole ineligibility upheld;

•

R. v.
Rushton
,

2000 YTCA 5
– 17 years’ parole ineligibility upheld;

•

R. v.
Atwal
,
2006
BCCA 493
– 16 years’ parole ineligibility upheld;

•

R. v.
Martel
,
2011
ABCA 225
– 12 years’ parole ineligibility increased to 15 years on appeal; and

•

R. v.
Praljak
,

2019 ONCA 394
– 15 years’ parole ineligibility upheld.

[
89
]

In all of these cases,
the offenders brutally murdered women they knew—either a spouse, a child or an
associate. All of the offenders were sentenced after trial.

[
90
]

In
Cerra
, the
offender brutally beat a young woman over a petty drug dispute. The “savage and
prolonged beating” took the matter into the 12–15 year ineligibility period
range. The offence was not committed on impulse or a burst of anger, rather the
offender drove the victim to a secluded place, beat her then drowned her in the
course of a drawn-out episode. The offender was momentarily interrupted by a
third party and then returned to his attack on the victim. It was the finding
of the deliberation involved in resuming the attack that was the particularly
egregious circumstance. Justice Donald concluded that the offender’s
persistence and deliberation manifest in the killing was what constituted
extraordinary aggravating factors that elevated the offence to the higher range
of 15–20 years’ parole ineligibility.

[
91
]

In
Trotman
, following
a trial, a 20-year parole ineligibility period was imposed on the offender who
had repeatedly stabbed the victim, holding her down for some of the offence,
likely after sexually assaulting the victim. Extreme violence of a sadistic
nature had been employed and the nature of the offence was described as having “an
element of vindictiveness and cruelty” to it. Significantly, the offender had a
record for violence and was on probation at the time he committed the offence.

[
92
]

In

Purdy
,
the
offender ambushed his estranged wife as she walked to work and stabbed her 21
times. The trial judge described the murder as brutal and concluded that the
circumstances established that the killing had elements of forethought and
pre-thought-out planning. Although the offender had no criminal record, there
was a protection order in place for the victim at the time of the offence, and
so there was a breach of that court order. The trial judge also found that the
circumstances surrounding the commission of the offence included months of
anger by the offender over the separation and the offender engaging in fear-inducing
harassment of the victim. Following the offence, he attempted to blame the
murder on someone else. Collectively these factors involved exceptional
aggravating circumstances that properly placed Mr. Purdy into the elevated
range of 15–20 years of parole ineligibility.

[
93
]

In
Rushton
, the
offender travelled from Nova Scotia to the Yukon to visit his young daughter.
He stabbed his estranged wife 20 times. The child was in the home when the
offence was committed. The offender made a statement at the time of the offence
that “no one will take my child from me”. Justice Braidwood described this
statement as showing a lack of concern for the child, and was indicative of “a
selfish need regardless of the consequences to the child to impose his will.” A
significantly aggravating circumstance in
Rushton
was the trial judge’s
finding that the offender did not endeavour to get assistance for his estranged
wife when friends attended at the door of the residence shortly after he had
stabbed the victim and she was still alive. The trial judge stated, “[t]he
possibility of help was there; he did not give it any thought whatsoever. I
find that chilling.”

[
94
]

Atwal
involved the offender stabbing his 17-year-old
daughter 17 times as she sat belted into the passenger seat of his vehicle. The
case is sometimes inaccurately referred to as an “honour killing.” There was
absolutely nothing honourable about it. The offender murdered his daughter as
she had continued to see her boyfriend, a young man not of the same faith and
someone the deceased’s father had directed her to discontinue seeing. The trial
judge found the motive for the offence
was the offender’s
anger at his daughter’s unwillingness to obey his directions to end her
relationship. Although the offender had no prior record and was an otherwise
contributing member of society, a finding that there was considerable
forethought, albeit short of planning and deliberation, placed the offender in
the range of sentence for offences with the highest order of moral culpability.

[
95
]

The decision in
Martel

is not from this province, nevertheless there are a few notable similarities to
the case at bar.
In
Martel
, the offender stabbed his wife once in the
abdomen and then made a video of her dying moments with his cell phone.
Dissimilar to the case at bar was the fact that the offender
in
Martel

spent months blaming others for the offence and lying to the police (para. 9).
As well, the offender had a prior, albeit dated, criminal record for both
spousal assault and uttering threats. The most significant aggravating factors
that concerned the Alberta Court of Appeal were the chilling and callous
conduct of the offender recording the deceased’s dying moments, his months of
blaming others and lying to the police, and his lack of insight into the
consequences of his conduct when he apologized to his family and the police for
his conduct, but made only ambivalent statements of regret to the deceased’s
family.

[
96
]

There is little
information about the full sentencing circumstances
in the case of
Praljak

apart from the fact that the offender stabbed his wife in the abdomen three
times. When discovered by his mother-in-law moments after the stabbing, he cut
his wrists causing life-threatening injuries. At the Ontario Court of Appeal,
no oral submissions were provided as to the fitness of the 15-year period of
parole ineligibility imposed after a jury convicted the offender of second
degree murder. The cryptic comments of the court dismissing the sentence appeal
noted that “[f]ifteen years of parole ineligibility falls within the range for
domestic homicide cases.” Respectfully, the decision is of little assistance in
this case.

Defence Counsel

[
97
]

In the case at bar, the
defence acknowledges that the accused’s conduct in this offence is horrifying
and that the primary principles of sentencing that inform the analysis are
deterrence and denunciation. However, the defence contends that with the
passage of time and some significant work on the part of Mr. Poepl while
detained in custody, he now has insight into his poor conduct and has taken
full responsibility for his actions. Mr. Poepl is prepared to accept whatever
sentence the Court imposes.

[
98
]

Mr. Poepl’s counsel
observed that “no human being is as bad as the worst thing they have ever
done.” Accordingly, the defence contends that when the nature of the offence
and the circumstances surrounding the commission of this murder are examined,
along with the character and background of Mr. Poepl, including his
demonstrated steps towards rehabilitation, when properly assessed within the governing
legal framework, the court should exercise mercy and not elevate the period of
parole ineligibility above the statutory minimum 10-year period.

[
99
]

Defence counsel relied
on the following cases to support their position:

•

R. v. Danjou
,
2020 BCSC 1820
– 12 years’ parole
ineligibility imposed following a judge alone trial;

•

R. v. Dolman
,
2017 BCSC 2564
– 11 years’ parole
ineligibility imposed following a guilty plea;

•

R. v. D.W.M.
,
2005 BCSC 1061
– 10 years’ parole
ineligibility imposed following a judge alone trial;

•

R. v. Forster
,
2012 BCSC 1682
– 12 years’ parole
ineligibility imposed following a guilty plea

•

R. v. Ghiorghita
,
2017 BCSC 1636
– 10 years’ parole
ineligibility imposed following a judge alone trial;

•

R. v. Hunter
,
2016 BCSC 796
– 11 years’ parole
ineligibility imposed following a jury trial;

•

R. v. Thomson
,
2019 BCSC 365
– 10 years’ parole ineligibility
imposed on a joint submission (accordingly I will not make any further
reference to this case);

•

R. v. Wu
,
2017 BCSC 2271
– 12 years’ parole
ineligibility imposed following a jury trial;

•

R. v. Waraich
,
2008 BCSC 919
– 10 years’ parole
ineligibility imposed following a jury trial.

[
100
]

Like the cases provided
by the Crown, in most of these cases, the offenders murdered women they knew—either
a spouse, a common-law partner, an intimate partner or an associate.

[
101
]

In
Danjou
, Justice
Beames imposed a parole ineligibility period of 12 years on the 71-year-old offender
who attacked and beat his common-law spouse after they had an argument earlier
in the afternoon in a vineyard they had been touring. After being directed to
get his own hotel room and told by the deceased that she would not give him a
ride back to Surrey, BC, the offender went to the deceased’s hotel room and
proceeded to beat her with a wine bottle. He hit her approximately 52 times, and
at some point the wine bottle broke. When a guest complained about noise, a
hotel employee attended at the hotel room, saw the deceased, who was still
alive, asking for help and showing signs of swelling to her face. The offender
told the employee that the deceased did not need help and the employee
retreated. The offender then continued his attack on his spouse. Some of the
injuries were cut and stab-like injuries consistent with being inflicted by the
broken wine bottle found at the scene.

[
102
]

The offender
in
Danjou

was a real estate broker with a history of domestic violence albeit no
criminal record. His spouse had tried to end the relationship and texted him to
that effect on several different occasions when they were separated. The
offender continued to attempt to maintain the relationship. He was diagnosed as
suffering from a delusional disorder jealous type, alcohol abuse disorder and
narcissistic personality traits, all of which contributed to the deterioration
of the marital relationship.

[
103
]

Justice Beames
noted in

Danjou
at para.
32
that the usual range of parole ineligibility imposed
in domestic/spousal homicide cases is 12–15 years. The cases she reviewed in
her reasons, many of which were also placed before the Court on Mr. Poepl’s
sentencing, clearly establish this point. It was the offender’s age, admission
that he killed his wife, and his remorse, that placed him at the bottom end of
the range:
Danjou
at para.
35
. There were no extraordinary aggravating
facts
in
Danjou
that moved the case into the higher elevated range

established in
Cerra
.

[
104
]

In
Dolman
, the
offender pled guilty to the second degree murder of the boyfriend of a sex
trade worker that the offender had a sexual relationship with, and during the
course of the relationship became much more involved with than a purely
transactional relationship. When the offender, who was 65 and had only one
prior unrelated conviction from when he was 28 years old, discovered that the
deceased and his girlfriend had stolen $600 from the offender while he was out
of his home, the offender felt betrayed and became enraged. He pursued the
couple and attacked the deceased in the parking lot of a Save-On-Foods store,
stabbing him multiple times in the chest. Justice Shergill described the attack
as an offence committed in a fit of rage by a socially isolated man who felt
betrayed by someone he cared for (para. 58). Although there were opportunities
for the offender to end his chase before he attacked the deceased, the offender
did not disengage.

[
105
]

The Crown contended
in
Dolman

that the offender was at the lower end of the 12–15 year range for parole
ineligibility and the defence argued that the minimum period of parole
ineligibility was warranted. In imposing an 11-year period of parole
ineligibility, it can be inferred that the sentencing judge determined that the
totality of the circumstances
in
Dolman
did not fit within the first
elevated range delineated
in
Cerra
.

[
106
]

In
D.W.M.
, the
offender was convicted after trial in relation to the shooting death of his
wife. Significantly, in that case there was no history of domestic violence
between the parties (para. 6). Even more significant was the fact that the
Crown did not seek the imposition of an elevated period of parole ineligibility
(para. 5). Accordingly, the case is of little assistance to the determination
that I must make in respect of Mr. Poepl.

[
107
]

In
Forster
, the
offender pled guilty to second degree murder in relation to her confinement and
stabbing her former young lover. The offender invited the deceased over for one
last get-together before she moved to Toronto. The deceased did not attend at
the offender’s apartment that night but did attend the next morning. The
offender and the deceased engaged in a consensual sex act with the deceased
tied and handcuffed to the bed. Thereafter, Ms. Forster attacked the deceased
with a knife and a hammer. The deceased was stabbed 32 times and beaten with
the hammer, both weapons were broken in the attack. The offender left the
apartment, went to a friend’s place, told him what had happened and then went
to the airport in an effort to leave the jurisdiction. The friend called the
police and the offender was arrested at the airport.

[
108
]

The offender, who had
had a very difficult background, a drug addiction and was a sex trade worker,
had no prior record. The offender was a transgender woman who was transitioning
at the time of her sentencing.

[
109
]

In conducting his
analysis of the s. 745.4 factors, Justice Schultes concluded that the
offence-related factors weighed in favour of an emphasis on deterrence and
denunciation (para. 50). The offence was found to be a massive, frenzied, and
protracted explosion of violence at a sometime romantic partner following
sexual contact, fuelled by anger at statements made by the deceased of his
ongoing commitment to another woman (para. 47). The character-related factors
tended to moderate somewhat the emphasis on deterrence and denunciation (para.
57). Nevertheless, after balancing everything, Schultes J. concluded that
although there were mitigating factors, they did not oust the need for an
elevated period of parole ineligibility (para. 58).

[
110
]

In
Ghiorghita
, the
38-year-old offender shot his wife in the abdomen eight times while she was
lying in bed. Psychiatric evidence adduced at his trial established that in the
weeks leading up to the offence, the offender experienced humiliation,
distress, anxiety and insomnia as his marriage unravelled. He felt betrayed by
his wife’s infidelity and betrayed again when she announced she intended to
continue her affair. The offender, who had no criminal record, was determined
to have a personality trait of over-controlled anger, obsessive personality
traits and traits of dependency and avoidance related to his marriage.

[
111
]

In
Ghiorghita
,

the trial judge specifically found that in leaving the victim without
calling for medical assistance, the offender was in a confused and highly distressed
state and that his abandonment of the victim was not a calculated choice to
leave her to bleed to death (paras. 34, 51). Balancing the competing objectives
of the need for deterrence and denunciation with the prospects for
rehabilitation and the low risk of reoffending led Justice Pearlman to conclude
that the period of parole ineligibility in that case did not need to be greater
than the statutory minimum.

[
112
]

In
Hunter
, the
60-year-old offender stabbed her close friend and drug supplier 21 times with a
kitchen steak knife. The offence occurred in the deceased’s apartment, where
the offender frequently went to visit and purchase heroin to support her
addiction. The offender also took a supply of heroin and approximately $1000
cash from the deceased’s home. Justice Holmes (as she then was) found that the
offender did nothing to ensure the deceased received medical assistance.
Indeed, she was also found to have taken steps to clean up the deceased’s
apartment before leaving. The jury rejected the offender’s claims of acting in
self-defence. While the jury recommended a 10 year period of parole
ineligibility, Holmes J. concluded that the length of the attack, coupled
with the evidence of gratuitous violence and the horrific circumstances that
the deceased endured in her final moments, necessitated the imposition of a period
of parole ineligibility of 11 years.

[
113
]

In
Wu
, the 44-year-old
offender murdered his wife by stabbing her with a cleaver-type knife used for
chopping vegetables. The couple were going through a very difficult period in
their marriage and on the day of the offence the deceased had excluded the
offender from a family function. The offender commenced the attack on the
deceased in their apartment, while the deceased’s 7-year-old daughter was in
the home. The daughter ran to a neighbour’s apartment asking for help. The
offender stabbed and chopped his wife approximately 250 times, and while the
attack started in the apartment, it continued in the hallway after the deceased
followed the offender out of the apartment. The description of the injuries and
the ferocity of the attack are disturbing. Although the offender had numerous
opportunities to stop his attack, he did not. By returning a verdict of
second-degree murder, the jury rejected the partial defence of provocation. The
jurors returned an array of recommendations for parole ineligibility ranging
from 10 years to 25 years. In the end, Justice Watchuk fixed the period of
parole ineligibility at 12 years, placing the offender in the lower range of
elevated parole ineligibility as there were aggravating circumstances.

[
114
]

In
Waraich
, the
24-year-old offender stabbed his wife 39 times after she uttered provocative
comments and threatened to return to India with their young son. The jury
recommended 10 years as the parole ineligibility period and Justice Wedge gave
significant weight to the recommendation. Indeed, Crown counsel made no
submission for an elevated parole ineligibility period.

[
115
]

The cases provided by
the defence illustrate that the range of parole ineligibility from the
statutory minimum to approximately 12 years occurs in the context of cases with
minimal aggravating circumstances and considerable prospects for
rehabilitation. Moreover, in some cases the Crown did not seek an elevated period
of ineligibility. While Mr. Poepl shows considerable prospects for
rehabilitation, it is the nature of the offence and the circumstances in which
it was committed that place his case above the range identified by the cases
provide by the defence.

Analysis

[
116
]

I turn first to address the aggravating and mitigating circumstances

Aggravating Circumstances

[
117
]

The Crown contends that the statutory aggravating circumstance
enumerated in
s. 718.2
(a)(iii) applies in this case—being that the evidence
establishes that the offender, in committing the offence, abused a position of
trust or authority in relation to the victim. With respect, I cannot agree with
that submission. Abuse of position of trust or authority cases deal primarily
with offences committed by adults where the victim is a child known to the
offender, e.g. teacher-student, doctor-patient, parent-child, or where the
offender holds a special position such as a lawyer in respect of trust funds or
the accountant for a victim company that has been defrauded.

[
118
]

In

Wu
, Watchuk J. rejected that the offender was in a
position of trust in respect of his wife whom he had stabbed to death. However,
in that case the statutory aggravating factor in
s. 718.2
(a)(ii) was available—in
committing the offence the offender abused his spouse or common-law partner.

[
119
]

Mr. Poepl was not in a common-law relationship with Ms. Hasselmann
at the time of her death, although they had been in what was described as an “on-again,
off-again” relationship of seven years’ duration. Prior to September 2019, the
Code

did not include as a statutory aggravating factor that the offence was
committed against the offender’s intimate partner.
Section 718.2
(a)(ii) of the
Code

was amended by Bill C-75, and as of September 19, 2019, it is a statutory
aggravating factor on sentence that an offender, in committing the offence,
abused the offender’s intimate partner, a term now defined in
s. 2
of the
Code

to include a current or former spouse, common-law partner and dating
partner. Although, Mr. Poepl committed this offence before
s. 718.2
(a)(ii) was
amended, in my view, the fact that Mr. Poepl committed this offence against his
former intimate partner is nevertheless an aggravating factor, and always has
been at common law.

[
120
]

Accordingly, the aggravating circumstances for this offence include
the following:

•

Mr. Poepl
committed this offence against his former intimate partner at a time when she
was endeavouring to extricate herself from their relationship.

•

Mr.
Poepl’s chilling behaviour in recording Ms. Hasselmann on his cell phone after
he had stabbed her 47 times and his calm, matter-of-fact conversation with her
wherein he blamed Ms. Hasselmann for the attack because she had “disrespected
him”.

•

Mr.
Poepl’s failure to render assistance or call for assistance, when it was
clearly apparent that Ms. Hasselmann was still alive, communicating and
struggling to breathe for approximately two hours after being so brutally
stabbed, can only be described as callous and cruel conduct that is extremely
aggravating in the circumstances.

•

Mr.
Poepl’s decision to leave Ms. Hasselmann in his vehicle for nearly two hours to
basically “bleed out” while he returned to his home to conduct online shopping
and banking is a further aggravating factor, in so far as it demonstrates his
indifference as to whether he had actually killed Ms. Hasselmann when he
stabbed her. It is also demonstrative of his intended course of conduct,
ensuring that Ms. Hasselmann died.

•

Mr.
Poepl’s continued purposive conduct to ensure Ms. Hasselmann died by keeping
her with him in the vehicle when he tried to take his own life by crashing the
vehicle.

•

Finally,
pursuant to
s. 718.2
(a)(iii.1) of the
Code
, the murder of Ms. Hasselmann
has severely impacted her family and friends, who are victims by virtue of
s. 2

of the
Code
, particularly her immediate family, being her young son, her
brother and her parents. The victim impact statements filed at the sentencing
hearing amply demonstrate the breadth of the emotional and psychological
devastation that they have experienced and will continue to experience for the
rest of their lives.

Mitigating Circumstances

[
121
]

The mitigating circumstances in this case include the following:

•

Mr. Poepl’s guilty plea and acceptance of
responsibility for this offence. This has saved the victim’s families the
trauma and uncertainty of having to go through a lengthy trial with horrific
details. They have been spared the gruelling ordeal of giving evidence in court
proceedings. Moreover, the justice system has been spared the burdens
associated with the trial.

•

Mr. Poepl’s demonstrated remorse not only
through his guilty plea but in his comments to the court and in his discussions
with family, friends and corrections authorities, including the prison chaplain
and a rabbi providing him with spiritual counselling and guidance.

•

Mr. Poepl’s exemplary behaviour while detained
in custody for this offence.

•

Mr. Poepl’s efforts at rehabilitation thus far,
which demonstrate a commitment to trying to make amends and to move forward
conducting himself in a more prosocial lifestyle.

•

Mr. Poepl’s lack of a criminal record prior to
this offence.

[
122
]

The jurisprudence mandates that when sentencing in a case like this,
where the offence involves violence inflicted upon one’s intimate partner, the
Court must give primary consideration to the objectives of denunciation and
deterrence of the conduct that forms the basis of the offence. Accordingly,
those objectives are accorded significant weight and the sentence I impose in
this case aims to achieve and honour that directive. Nevertheless, I cannot
ignore the objective of rehabilitation in this case as Mr. Poepl has made
significant steps to better himself while detained in custody.

[
123
]

The Crown contends that this case “could not be closer to first
degree murder” and that the elements of forethought, calculation and
deliberation are all present. I agree that when assessed on the wide spectrum
of cases that comprise the offence of second degree murder, this case is closer
to first degree murder than it is manslaughter. However, it is, respectfully, in
my view a difficult proposition to accept a plea to second degree murder and
then essentially argue that the case is a first degree murder case.

[
124
]

What I take from the facts as to the nature and circumstances of the
offence is that Mr. Poepl became enraged at Ms. Hasselmann and her refusal to
continue a romantic relationship with him. While the act of stabbing Ms.
Hasselmann may have had an element of impulsive rage, it was not without
forethought to the consequences of what he was doing. Moreover, u
nlike the circumstances
in
Ghiorghita
,
the evidence here supports the inference that Mr. Poepl did choose to abandon
Ms. Hasselmann who was still very much alive, but severely wounded, and return
to his home to engage in what might be described as putting his affairs in
order.

[
125
]

Mr. Poepl’s moral blameworthiness for this offence is extremely
elevated given his overall course of conduct that commenced with the stabbing, but
did not end there. Rather, his conduct continued in a callous, calculated
fashion wherein he ignored Ms. Hasselmann’s plight when she possibly could have
been saved. Instead, he focused on his own personal circumstances. Reinforcing
this conclusion is Mr. Poepl’s decision to try and kill himself to avoid legal
jeopardy, and in doing so deciding to take Ms. Hasselmann (who at that point
was still alive) with him in the intentional motor vehicle accident. While Ms.
Hasselmann no doubt was gravely injured by the stab wounds sustained,
particularly to her thyroid, an early intervention and call for assistance may
have resulted in a different outcome for her. Mr. Poepl did not adopt that
course of conduct. Much like the circumstances described by Justice Satanove in

Trotman
, there is an element of cruelty and vindictiveness which can be
inferred by the nature and overall circumstances surrounding the murder of Ms.
Hasselmann.

[
126
]

I respectfully disagree with the Crown that Mr. Poepl’s otherwise
good antecedents and the other mitigating factors are completely overwhelmed by
the callousness of his conduct in committing this offence. If that were so then
the individualized approach to sentencing in cases such as this would simply
focus on the nature of the offence and the circumstances of its commission.
Such an approach is not supported in the jurisprudence or the governing
legislation. Rather, sentencing in cases like this is always a delicate
balancing of all factors, as well as the objectives and principles of sentencing.

[
127
]

The range of parole ineligibility in cases of domestic/spousal
homicide or intimate partner homicide where there are aggravating factors, as
there are here, is at least 12–15 years as the authorities establish:
Danjou

at para.
32
.

[
128
]

Much like the circumstances and the question in
Cerra

at para.

17
, the key issue in Mr. Poepl’s case is whether there was something more in
this case that lifts it into a still higher level of moral blameworthiness such
that it moves into the further elevated range of parole ineligibility of 15–20
years.

[
129
]

In this case I find that there are several extraordinary aggravating
factors here that include:

i.

Mr. Poepl’s chilling and callous attitude toward
Ms. Hasselmann in his recording her struggling for breath after he stabbed her
repeatedly;

ii.

Mr. Poepl’s conduct of blaming Ms. Hasselmann
for being the cause of the attack because she disrespected him;

iii.

Mr. Poepl’s abject failure to render or obtain
any assistance after he repeatedly stabbed Ms. Hasselmann; and

iv.

Leaving Ms. Hasselmann to suffer in the vehicle
for two hours.

[
130
]

These four points constitute extremely aggravating circumstances and
establish Mr. Poepl’s extremely elevated state of moral blameworthiness. These
findings place this case in the higher elevated range of parole ineligibility established
in
Cerra

and reinforced in
Bennight
.

[
131
]

It is Mr. Poepl’s antecedents, his genuine remorse and his guilty
plea, as well as his developed insight and his work on himself since this
offence, all of which support the conclusion that there are prospects for
rehabilitation, that militate in favour of placing him at the bottom of that
range. Thus, similar to the observations of Schultes J. in
Forster
, Mr.
Poepl’s personal factors, including his genuine remorse and his guilty plea, are
far from inconsequential in this analysis, and it is those personal factors that
keep the period of parole ineligibility at the bottom of the higher enhanced
range set out in
Cerra
.

[
132
]

Anything lower than 15 years would not accurately reflect the
heightened moral culpability inherent in the egregious and callous manner that
this murder was carried out, and would give insufficient recognition to the
pressing need for denunciation and general deterrence that arises from this
case.

Sentence

133
]
